chapter_note.about: Logic is the language for saying exactly when something is true. This chapter starts with statements joined by and, or, not and if-then, and shows how a truth table tests them. Next come the labels tautology and contradiction, and how to translate English into formulas. The second half adds 'for all' and 'there exists', with negation, translation, pulling a quantifier past an implication, and checking sentences on small domains. GATE questions are short: translate, simplify, or find the one row or element that breaks a claim.
chapter_note.simple: Logic is a careful way to say when a sentence is true. Facts joined by 'and', 'or', 'not' and 'if-then' can be checked row by row in a table. A sentence that is always true is a tautology, and one that is never true is a contradiction. The words 'for all' and 'there is' talk about a whole group. To argue against 'for all' you just need one counterexample, and to prove 'there is' you need one example. English words like 'only if' and 'unless' hide an arrow, and you must decide which way it points. When in doubt, test on a tiny case.

cards.title: Connectives and truth tables
cards.simple: Take the sentence 'it is raining and I have an umbrella'. Whether it is true depends on two simple facts. A truth table lists every combination of those facts (rain yes or no, umbrella yes or no) and says if the whole sentence is true in each one. 'And' needs both facts true, 'or' needs at least one, and 'not' flips a fact. Two facts give 4 rows, three facts give 8 rows. You work out the sentence in small pieces, one column at a time. In exam words: a truth table evaluates a compound proposition under all assignments to its variables.
cards.idea: A compound statement is made of simple true/false statements joined by connectives such as **and**, **or**, **not** and **if-then**. To see exactly when it is true, list every combination of truth values and compute the result row by row. That list is a **truth table**.
cards.definition:
Connectives, with $p,q$ true/false statements:

- $\neg p$ (not): flips the value.
- $p\wedge q$ (and): true only if both are true.
- $p\vee q$ (or): true if at least one is true (inclusive).
- $p\to q$ (if $p$ then $q$): false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.
- $p\leftrightarrow q$ (iff): true when $p$ and $q$ have the same value.

Precedence, tightest first: $\neg,\ \wedge,\ \vee,\ \to,\ \leftrightarrow$. A formula with $n$ variables has $2^n$ rows.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each variable as a switch that is on (T) or off (F). The formula is a small circuit built from gates: NOT, AND, OR. A truth table is the circuit's output for every setting of the switches. The reliable way to fill it is column by column: first the inputs, then each sub-formula in the order you would compute it by hand, and the final column last. The implication $p\to q$ is the one that surprises people. It is a promise: 'if $p$ happens, then $q$ happens'. The promise is only broken when $p$ happens and $q$ does not. If $p$ never happens, nothing is broken, so $p\to q$ is true. That is why $F\to q$ is true for any $q$. Precedence matters too. Without brackets, $\wedge$ binds tighter than $\vee$, just as $\times$ binds tighter than $+$.

examples.setup: Build the truth table of $(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)$ and describe when it is true.
steps: Two variables give 4 rows: TT, TF, FT, FF for $(p,q)$.
Column $p\vee q$ is true if at least one is true: T, T, T, F.
Column $p\wedge q$ is true only when both are true: T, F, F, F.
Column $\neg(p\wedge q)$ flips that: F, T, T, T.
AND the columns $p\vee q$ and $\neg(p\wedge q)$: F, T, T, F.
examples.answer: The formula is true exactly when $p$ and $q$ have different values (exclusive or): rows TF and FT.

examples.setup: For how many of the 8 assignments to $(p,q,r)$ is $(p\to q)\wedge(q\to r)$ true?
steps: There are $2^3=8$ rows. The formula needs both implications true.
$p\to q$ is false when $p=T$ and $q=F$: rows TFT and TFF are out.
$q\to r$ is false when $q=T$ and $r=F$: rows TTF and FTF are out.
These two groups share no row, so $8-2-2=4$ rows remain: TTT, FTT, FFT, FFF.
Reading the survivors: the values never go from T back to F, so it is a chain $p\Rightarrow q\Rightarrow r$.
examples.answer: 4 assignments.

examples.setup: How many of the 8 assignments make $\neg p\vee q\wedge r$ true, and how many make $(\neg p\vee q)\wedge r$ true?
steps: Without brackets, $\wedge$ binds tighter than $\vee$, so the first formula is $\neg p\vee(q\wedge r)$.
It is true whenever $p=F$ (4 rows), plus the row $p=T,q=T,r=T$. That is $4+1=5$.
The second formula needs $r=T$ and $(\neg p\vee q)$. With $r=T$ the pairs $(p,q)$ that work are TT, FT, FF: 3 rows.
The same symbols give 5 or 3 depending on brackets.
examples.answer: 5 for $\neg p\vee(q\wedge r)$ and 3 for $(\neg p\vee q)\wedge r$. Always apply precedence or add brackets first.

how: Count the variables and write $2^n$ rows.
Add one column for each sub-formula, in the order you would evaluate by hand.
Use the rules: $\wedge$ needs both, $\vee$ needs one, $p\to q$ fails only on TF.
Apply precedence ($\neg$, then $\wedge$, then $\vee$, then $\to$) before you compute.
If values are forced (for example $r=F$), drop the rows that contradict them.

cards.title: Implication and equivalences
cards.simple: Say your friend promises: 'If it rains, I will bring an umbrella.' The promise is broken only if it rains and the friend has no umbrella. If it does not rain, nothing is broken, whether the friend has an umbrella or not. Now flip the promise around two ways. 'If no umbrella, then no rain' says exactly the same thing. 'If umbrella, then rain' is a different promise. A truth table shows this: the first two have identical columns and the third does not. In exam words: p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p ≡ ¬p∨q, but the converse q→p is not equivalent.
cards.idea:
An implication $p	o q$ is a promise that is broken only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. It has two equivalent forms: the **contrapositive** $
eg q	o
eg p$ and the **or-form** $
eg p\vee q$. The **converse** $q	o p$ and the **inverse** $
eg p	o
eg q$ are not equivalent to it.

$$p	o q\ \equiv\ 
eg p\vee q\ \equiv\ 
eg q	o
eg p$$

Converse of $p	o q$: $q	o p$. Inverse: $
eg p	o
eg q$. The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, but not to $p	o q$.

$p\leftrightarrow q\equiv(p	o q)\wedge(q	o p)$. De Morgan: $
eg(p\wedge q)\equiv
eg p\vee
eg q$ and $
eg(p\vee q)\equiv
eg p\wedge

cards.intuition_full:
Equivalent means the two formulas have the same truth value in every row of the table. So the test for an equivalence is always: compare the final columns. The contrapositive works because both formulas are broken in exactly one case. $p	o q$ breaks when $p=T,q=F$. $
eg q	o
eg p$ breaks when $
eg q=T$ and $
eg p=F$, which is again $q=F,p=T$. Same row, same formula. The or-form $
eg p\vee q$ says the same thing in different words: either $p$ does not happen, or $q$ does. It is false only when $p$ happens and $q$ does not. The converse swaps the roles and breaks in a different row ($p=F,q=T$), so it is a different statement. A good habit: when two forms look similar, ask 'in which single row does each one fail?'.

cards.title: Tautology, contradiction and satisfiability
cards.simple: Some sentences are true no matter what, like 'it will rain or it will not rain'. Some are never true, like 'it is raining and it is not raining'. Most are true in some situations and false in others. To sort a formula, look at every row of its truth table. All rows true means a tautology, all rows false means a contradiction, and at least one true row means satisfiable. A quick trick: try to make the formula false, and if you cannot, it is a tautology. In exam words: tautology, contradiction and contingency are decided by the final column of the table.
cards.idea: Look at the final column of a truth table. **All true** means a tautology. **All false** means a contradiction. **At least one true** means satisfiable. If it is true in some rows and false in others, it is neither a tautology nor a contradiction. The fast test is to try to make the formula false.
cards.definition:
- **Tautology:** true in every row.
- **Contradiction:** false in every row.
- **Satisfiable:** true in at least one row.
- **Contingent:** true in some rows and false in others.

Link: $f$ is a tautology iff $\neg f$ is unsatisfiable. $f$ is satisfiable iff $\neg f$ is not a tautology.
cards.intuition_full: A tautology is a statement with no way to fail. So the quickest test is to try to build a failing row. Assume the formula is false, push that assumption through the connectives, and see if the values contradict each other. If they do, no failing row exists, and the formula is a tautology. If you reach a consistent assignment, that assignment is a counterexample. This 'falsify' method is much shorter than writing all $2^n$ rows when there are 3 or more variables. The dual idea is satisfiability: try to make the formula true. Contradictions are the mirror image of tautologies, and negating one gives the other. A formula that is true in some rows and false in others is called contingent: it describes a real situation, not a law of logic.

examples.setup: Is $(p\to q)\to\big((p\wedge r)\to(q\wedge r)\big)$ a tautology?
steps: Try to make it false. An implication is false only when the left side is true and the right side is false.
Left side true: $p\to q$ is true.
Right side false: $p\wedge r$ is true and $q\wedge r$ is false. So $p=T$, $r=T$, and then $q$ must be $F$.
But then $p\to q=T\to F=F$, which contradicts the left side being true.
No failing row exists.
examples.answer: Yes, it is a tautology (no row makes it false).

cards.title: English to propositional logic
cards.simple: Say a teacher says, 'You can go out to play only if you finish your homework.' Going out is only allowed when homework is done. So if you are out playing, your homework must be done. The sentence says 'out → homework', and not 'homework → out', because finishing homework does not force you to go out. Words like 'only if', 'if', 'unless' and 'when' all hide an arrow, and the trick is to decide which way it points. Test the sentence by asking which single situation would break the promise. In exam words: 'p only if q' is p→q; 'p if q' is q→p; 'p unless q' is ¬q→p.
cards.idea: English hides the logical arrow in words like **if**, **only if**, **unless** and **when**. The skill is to find which statement is the condition and which is the result. Then test your formula by asking which one case would break the sentence.
cards.definition:
Translations, with $p,q$ statements:

- 'if $p$ then $q$', '$q$ if $p$', '$q$ whenever $p$', '$p$ implies $q$': $p\to q$.
- '$p$ only if $q$': $p\to q$.
- '$p$ is sufficient for $q$': $p\to q$. '$p$ is necessary for $q$': $q\to p$.
- '$p$ if and only if $q$': $p\leftrightarrow q$.
- '$p$ unless $q$': $\neg q\to p$, which is equivalent to $p\vee q$.
- '$p$ but $q$': $p\wedge q$.
cards.intuition_full: 'If' introduces the thing that is enough. 'Only if' introduces the thing that is needed. 'The match is cancelled only if it rains' says rain is needed for cancellation. So cancellation brings rain along with it: $c\to r$. 'If it rains, the match is cancelled' says rain is enough to cancel: $r\to c$. The directions are opposite. A reliable check is to ask which situation makes the sentence false, and write the formula that fails in exactly that row. For 'cancelled only if rain', the breaking case is cancelled on a dry day: $c\wedge\neg r$. The implication $c\to r$ fails only at $c=T,r=F$. It matches. 'Unless' means 'if not': 'A unless B' is 'if not B then A'. This is the same as 'A or B'. Negations inside the sentence ('cannot', 'not') change the formula only for the part they attach to.

examples.setup: Let $r$ = 'it rains' and $c$ = 'the match is cancelled'. Write 'The match is cancelled **only if** it rains' in logic. How is it different from 'If it rains, the match is cancelled'?
steps: Name the atoms: $r$ = it rains, $c$ = the match is cancelled.
'$c$ only if $r$': rain is needed for cancellation, so $c\to r$.
The one case that breaks the sentence is cancelled on a dry day: $c=T,\ r=F$. That is the only row where $c\to r$ is false.
'If it rains, the match is cancelled' is $r\to c$, which points the other way and is a different statement.
examples.answer: $c\to r$. It differs from $r\to c$ (the converse).

examples.setup: Let $l$ = 'a student leaves the hall', $s$ = 'the student has submitted', $i$ = 'the invigilator permits it'. Write 'A student leaves **only if** they have submitted **and** the invigilator permits'. In how many of the 8 assignments is it true?
steps: 'Only if' puts the leaving on the left: $l\to(\ldots)$.
Both conditions are needed together, so the right side is $s\wedge i$. Formula: $l\to(s\wedge i)$.
Count the true rows. If $l=F$ the implication is true for all 4 choices of $(s,i)$.
If $l=T$, it is true only when $s=T$ and $i=T$: 1 row.
$4+1=5$ rows. The wrong reading $(s\wedge i)\to l$ would force leaving, which the sentence never says.
examples.answer: $l\to(s\wedge i)$, true in 5 of 8 assignments.

eg m$ and B = $r$: $
eg r	o
eg m$.

eg r	o m$ (equivalently $r\vee m$). (b) $
eg r	o
eg m$ (equivalently $m	o r$).

cards.title: Quantifiers and negation
cards.simple: 'Every student passed something' is a claim about a whole class. To prove it false you do not need to check everyone, you only need to find one student who passed nothing. That is how negation works with 'every' and 'some'. The opposite of 'everyone has it' is 'someone does not have it'. The opposite of 'someone has it' is 'nobody has it'. When there are two quantifiers, you flip both and negate the thing at the end. Their order also matters: 'everyone has a friend' is not the same as 'someone is everybody's friend'. In exam words: ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P, ¬∃x P ≡ ∀x ¬P, and ∃x∀y implies ∀y∃x but not the reverse.
cards.idea: A **quantifier** says how many elements of the domain satisfy a predicate: $\forall$ means 'all', $\exists$ means 'at least one'. To negate a quantified statement, **flip every quantifier** ($\forall\leftrightarrow\exists$) and **negate the predicate** at the end. The order of different quantifiers matters.
cards.definition:
$$
eg orall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,
eg P(x)\qquad
eg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv orall x\,
eg P(x)$$

For several quantifiers, move $
eg$ inward one quantifier at a time: $
eg orall x\,\exists y\,R\equiv\exists x\, orall y\,
eg R$.

Same quantifiers can swap: $ orall x orall y\equiv orall y orall x$ and $\exists x\exists y\equiv\exists y\exists x$. Mixed ones cannot: $\exists x orall y\,R\ \Rightarrow\  orall y\exists x\,R$, but not the reverse.
cards.intuition_full:
'For all' is a very strong claim: it survives only if no element breaks it. So it fails as soon as one element does, and 'not for all' is exactly 'there is a counterexample'. That is $
eg orall\equiv\exists
eg$. Likewise 'there exists' is a search for one witness, and 'not exists' means every candidate fails: $
eg\exists\equiv orall
eg$. Think of $ orall$ as a big AND over the domain, and $\exists$ as a big OR. De Morgan flips AND and OR when you negate, which is the same flip of quantifiers. For mixed quantifiers, read left to right as a game. In $ orall x\,\exists y$, you are given any $x$ first, and then you may pick $y$ to suit it. In $\exists x\, orall y$ you must pick $x$ first, and it has to work for every $y$. The second game is harder for you, so $\exists orall$ is the stronger statement: it implies $ orall\exists$ but not the reverse.

examples.setup: Students s1, s2, s3 and exams a, b. s1 passed a and b. s2 passed a. s3 passed nothing. Is 'every student passed some exam' true? Write its negation.
steps: Statement S: $\forall s\,\exists e\,\mathrm{Passed}(s,e)$. Think of lines between students and exams.
s1 has a line to a (and b), and s2 has a line to a. Both are fine.
s3 has no line, so there is no exam $e$ with $\mathrm{Passed}(s3,e)$. S is false.
Negation: flip $\forall s$ to $\exists s$, flip $\exists e$ to $\forall e$, negate inside: $\exists s\,\forall e\,\neg\mathrm{Passed}(s,e)$. Some student passed nothing. The witness is s3.
examples.answer: S is false. The negation $\exists s\,\forall e\,\neg\mathrm{Passed}(s,e)$ is true.

examples.setup: Domain $\{1,2,3\}$ and $R(x,y)$ means $x\ne y$. Evaluate $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ and $\exists y\,\forall x\,R(x,y)$.
steps: First: $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\ne y)$. For any $x$, pick a different $y$. For $x=1$ pick 2, for $x=2$ pick 1, for $x=3$ pick 1. True.
Second: $\exists y\,\forall x\,(x\ne y)$. We need one $y$ that differs from every $x$, including $x=y$ itself.
Whatever $y$ you pick, the choice $x=y$ breaks it. False.
So ($\forall\exists$ true, $\exists\forall$ false): the order of mixed quantifiers matters.
examples.answer: First is true, second is false. $\exists\forall$ implies $\forall\exists$ but not the reverse.

examples.setup: Is $\exists x\,\forall y\,(x\le y)$ true over the natural numbers $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$? Over the integers?
steps: Over the naturals pick $x=0$. Then $0\le y$ for every natural $y$. True.
Over the integers there is no smallest number. Whatever $x$ you pick, $y=x-1$ is smaller. False.
The negation over the integers is $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y<x)$, which is true.
The same sentence is true or false depending on the domain.
examples.answer: True over the naturals, false over the integers. The truth of a quantified sentence depends on the domain.

cards.title: English to first-order logic
cards.simple: Say we look at four things: a sparrow, an eagle, a bat and a rock. 'All birds fly' only talks about the birds. The rock is not a bird, so it cannot break the claim. In logic that is the arrow: 'if it is a bird, then it flies', and the rock passes by default. If you wrote 'it is a bird and it flies' for every item, you would be saying the rock is a flying bird. For 'some bird flies' you do want 'and', because you need a real flying bird to exist. In exam words: universal statements use ∀ with →, existential statements use ∃ with ∧.
cards.idea: Translate English into first-order logic by picking the quantifier, then the connective that fits it. **'All A are B'** uses $\forall$ with an arrow. **'Some A is B'** uses $\exists$ with an AND. Mixing these up is the most common mistake.
cards.definition:
With predicates $A(x),B(x)$:

- 'All $A$ are $B$': $\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))$.
- 'Some $A$ is $B$': $\exists x\,(A(x)\wedge B(x))$.
- 'No $A$ is $B$': $\neg\exists x\,(A(x)\wedge B(x))\equiv\forall x\,(A(x)\to\neg B(x))$.
- 'Exactly one $x$ has $P$': $\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge\forall y\,(P(y)\to y=x)\big)$.
cards.intuition_full: Read $\forall x\,(A\to B)$ as 'go through every element; for those that are $A$, check $B$; ignore the rest'. The arrow does the ignoring: when $A(x)$ is false the arrow is true, so non-$A$ elements never cause trouble. If you used $\wedge$ instead, you would require every element to be $A$ and $B$, which says far more than you meant. For $\exists$ the opposite holds. You need an element that is $A$ and also $B$. If you used $\to$, any element that is not $A$ would satisfy it automatically, and the sentence would be true for nearly any domain (this is called a trivial witness). 'Exactly one' needs two parts: existence (one $x$ has $P$) and uniqueness (any $y$ with $P$ is that same $x$). Several quantifiers in English are read in order: 'every student has a friend' puts $\forall$ on student first, then $\exists$ on friend.

examples.setup: Domain: sparrow, eagle, bat, rock. $B(x)$: $x$ is a bird; $F(x)$: $x$ can fly. Birds are the sparrow and eagle; flyers are the sparrow, eagle and bat. Is 'all birds fly' true? Why is $\forall x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$ a wrong translation?
steps: Fill $B$: T, T, F, F. Fill $F$: T, T, T, F (for sparrow, eagle, bat, rock).
'All birds fly' is $\forall x\,(B(x)\to F(x))$. For bat and rock $B$ is false, so the arrow is automatically true.
Row $B\to F$ is T, T, T, T. The statement is true.
$\forall x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$ says every item is a flying bird: row $B\wedge F$ is T, T, F, F. It is false, so it is a wrong translation.
'Some bird flies' needs $\wedge$: $\exists x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$, true with witness sparrow.
examples.answer: True with $\forall x\,(B\to F)$. The $\wedge$ version would also demand that the bat and the rock are flying birds.

examples.setup: Domain $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Using $P(x)$ for 'x is even', test 'exactly one x is even', and then use $P(x)$ for 'x > 3' and test it again.
steps: Formula: $\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge\forall y\,(P(y)\to y=x)\big)$. Existence plus uniqueness.
$P$ = even: the even elements are 2 and 4. Existence holds, but uniqueness fails: take $x=2$, then $y=4$ has $P(4)$ and $4\ne2$. False.
$P$ = '$>3$': only $x=4$ has $P$. Existence holds with $x=4$, and every $y$ with $P(y)$ equals 4. True.
A common wrong answer, $\exists x\,P(x)\wedge\forall y\,P(y)$, is a different statement: it says everything has $P$.
examples.answer: Even: false (2 and 4). 'x > 3': true (only 4).

examples.setup: A domain has no unicorns. Is $\forall x\,(\mathrm{Unicorn}(x)\to\mathrm{Flies}(x))$ true? Is $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Unicorn}(x)\to\mathrm{Flies}(x))$ a good way to say 'some unicorn flies'?
steps: With no unicorns, every $x$ makes $\mathrm{Unicorn}(x)$ false, so every implication is true.
So $\forall x\,(\mathrm{Unicorn}\to\mathrm{Flies})$ is true (vacuously).
For $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Unicorn}(x)\to\mathrm{Flies}(x))$, any $x$ that is not a unicorn already satisfies the arrow. It is true even though no unicorn flies.
To say 'some unicorn flies' use $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Unicorn}(x)\wedge\mathrm{Flies}(x))$, which is false here.
examples.answer: The $\forall$ statement is vacuously true. The $\exists$ with an arrow is a bad translation. Use $\wedge$ with $\exists$.

'No $A$ is $B$' is $\forall x\,(A\to\neg B)$.
'Exactly one' uses equality: $y=x$.
'At least two': $\exists x\exists y\,(x\ne y\wedge P(x)\wedge P(y))$.

- 'No $A$ is $B$': $\neg\exists x\,(A(x)\wedge B(x))\equiv\forall x\,(A(x)\to\neg B(x))$.
- 'Exactly one $x$ has $P$': $\exists x\,\big(P(x)\wedge\forall y\,(P(y)\to y=x)\big)$.

**Worked example.** Domain: sparrow, eagle, bat, rock. $B(x)$: $x$ is a bird; $F(x)$: $x$ can fly. Birds are the sparrow and eagle; flyers are the sparrow, eagle and bat. Is 'all birds fly' true? Why is $\forall x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$ a wrong translation?

1. Fill $B$: T, T, F, F. Fill $F$: T, T, T, F (for sparrow, eagle, bat, rock).
2. 'All birds fly' is $\forall x\,(B(x)\to F(x))$. For bat and rock $B$ is false, so the arrow is automatically true.
3. Row $B\to F$ is T, T, T, T. The statement is true.
4. $\forall x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$ says every item is a flying bird: row $B\wedge F$ is T, T, F, F. It is false, so it is a wrong translation.
5. 'Some bird flies' needs $\wedge$: $\exists x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$, true with witness sparrow.

**Answer:** True with $\forall x\,(B\to F)$. The $\wedge$ version would also demand that the bat and the rock are flying birds.

cards.title: Pulling a quantifier out past W
cards.simple: Say P(x) means 'student x passed' and W is a fact with nothing to do with any student, like 'the school is open'. The statement 'for every student, if they passed then the school is open' sounds like a rule about each student. But it only fails if some student passed while the school is closed. So it means 'if some student passed, then the school is open'. The word 'every' turned into 'some' because the student part sits in the 'if' side. When the student part is on the 'then' side, 'every' stays 'every'. In exam words: ∀x(P(x)→W) ≡ (∃xP(x))→W, because the quantifier flips when it moves out of the antecedent.
cards.idea: If $W$ does not mention $x$, you can pull a quantifier out of a formula that contains $W$. For $\wedge$ and $\vee$ the quantifier stays the same. For an implication, the quantifier **flips when it leaves the antecedent**, and stays the same when it leaves the consequent.
cards.definition:
Assume $W$ has no free occurrence of $x$ (and the domain is non-empty). Then:

- $\forall x\,(P\wedge W)\equiv\forall x\,P\wedge W$ and $\exists x\,(P\wedge W)\equiv\exists x\,P\wedge W$ (same for $\vee$)
- $\forall x\,(P\to W)\equiv\exists x\,P\to W$
- $\exists x\,(P\to W)\equiv\forall x\,P\to W$
- $\forall x\,(W\to P)\equiv W\to\forall x\,P$ and $\exists x\,(W\to P)\equiv W\to\exists x\,P$
cards.intuition_full:
Write the arrow as an or-form: $P	o W\equiv
eg P\vee W$. Then $ orall x\,(
eg P(x)\vee W)$. Since $W$ has no $x$, it can be taken out of a $ orall$ over an OR: $ orall x\,
eg P(x)\vee W$. And $ orall x\,
eg P(x)\equiv
eg\exists x\,P(x)$. So we get $
eg\exists x\,P(x)\vee W$, which is $\exists x\,P(x)	o W$. The flip comes from the negation hidden inside the arrow's left side. In plain words, $ orall x\,(P(x)	o W)$ only fails when some $x$ has $P(x)$ true and $W$ false. That is the same as 'if there is any $x$ with $P$, then $W$ must hold'. When $x$ sits on the right of the arrow ($W	o P(x)$) there is no negation on it, so the quantifier keeps its type. The condition that $W$ has no $x$ is essential: if $W$ depends on $x$, you cannot pull it out.

examples.setup: Domain $\{1,2,3\}$. $P(x)$: 'x is even'. $W$ is a fact with no $x$, and $W$ is false. Check that $\forall x\,(P(x)\to W)$ and $(\exists x\,P(x))\to W$ have the same value.
steps: $P(x)$ for $x=1,2,3$: F, T, F. $W$ is false in every column.
$P(x)\to W$: T, F, T. It fails at $x=2$.
$\forall x\,(P(x)\to W)$ is false, because $x=2$ fails.
$\exists x\,P(x)$ is true (x = 2). True → false is false. Same value.
Rule: $\forall x\,(P(x)\to W)\equiv(\exists x\,P(x))\to W$ when $W$ has no $x$.
examples.answer: Both are false. The quantifier flips from $\forall$ to $\exists$ when it leaves the antecedent.

examples.setup: $W$ has no free $x$. Which of these are valid equivalences? (1) $\exists x\,(P(x)\to W)\equiv\forall x\,P(x)\to W$. (2) $\forall x\,(W\to P(x))\equiv W\to\forall x\,P(x)$. (3) $\forall x\,(P(x)\to W)\equiv\forall x\,P(x)\to W$. (4) $\exists x\,(P(x)\vee W)\equiv\exists x\,P(x)\vee W$.
steps: (1) $P$ is in the antecedent and the quantifier moves out, so it flips: $\exists\to\forall$. Valid.
(2) $P$ is in the consequent: the quantifier does not flip. Valid.
(3) $P$ is in the antecedent but the quantifier stays $\forall$. It should flip to $\exists$. Invalid.
Counterexample for (3): domain $\{1,2\}$ with $P(1)=T,\ P(2)=F$ and $W=F$. Left: $x=1$ gives $T\to F=F$, so it is false. Right: $\forall x\,P(x)$ is false, so $F\to F=T$. Different values.
(4) For $\vee$ the quantifier stays the same. Valid.
examples.answer: (1), (2) and (4) are valid; (3) is not.

examples.setup: What if $W$ does mention $x$? Take $W=Q(x)$ and ask whether $\forall x\,(P(x)\to Q(x))\equiv(\exists x\,P(x))\to Q(x)$.
steps: The right side has a free $x$. It is not even a sentence, so it cannot equal the left side, which is a sentence.
Concretely, take the domain $\{1,2\}$ with $P(x)=Q(x)=$ '$x=1$'. The left side is true: $P(1)\to Q(1)=T$ and $P(2)\to Q(2)=F\to F=T$.
On the right, $\exists x\,P(x)$ is true, so its value is just $Q(x)$, which depends on which $x$ you test: true for $x=1$, false for $x=2$.
So the pull-out rules need $W$ to have no free $x$.
examples.answer: No. The rule applies only when $W$ has no free occurrence of $x$.

cards.title: Small domains and models
cards.simple: A sentence with 'for all' and 'there is' can be checked on a tiny world by hand. Say the world has just three numbers, 1, 2 and 3, and the sentence is 'every number has a bigger number'. Go through the numbers one by one. 1 has a bigger one, 2 has a bigger one, but 3 does not. One number failing is enough to make 'every' false. A tiny world where a sentence is true is called a model. Questions often ask how small such a world can be, or how many different worlds are possible. In exam words: a model is a domain with interpretations that make the sentence true; evaluate ∀ as AND and ∃ as OR over the domain.
cards.idea: A first-order sentence is true or false **in a particular domain**. On a small domain you can test it by going through the elements: $\forall$ is a big AND and $\exists$ is a big OR. A **model** of a sentence is a domain and relation that make it true. Some questions ask for the smallest model, or count the relations that satisfy a sentence.
cards.definition:
Over a finite domain $D=\{d_1,\dots,d_n\}$:

$$\forall x\,P(x)\equiv P(d_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge P(d_n)\qquad\exists x\,P(x)\equiv P(d_1)\vee\cdots\vee P(d_n)$$

A **model** of a sentence $\varphi$ is a domain $D$ with an interpretation of the predicate symbols such that $\varphi$ is true. A binary relation $R$ on $D$ is a set of ordered pairs, and there are $2^{n^2}$ of them.
cards.intuition_full: The rule of thumb is: think of the relation as an $n\times n$ table of 0s and 1s, where row $x$ and column $y$ say whether $R(x,y)$ holds. Then $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ says that every row has at least one 1. And $\exists x\,\forall y\,R(x,y)$ says that some row is all 1s. Once you see the table, counting relations is counting 0/1 tables with a row condition. For model-size questions, the key idea is witnesses. A sentence that starts $\exists x\forall y\ldots$ or needs only a bounded number of witnesses can be satisfied by a small subset of any model. If a sentence forces an endless chain (every element has a different larger element, with no repeats allowed), then no finite domain works. Finite domains cannot hold an infinite chain, so the pigeonhole principle forces a repeat.

examples.setup: Domain $\{1,2,3\}$ and $R(x,y)$ means $x<y$. Is $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ true?
steps: Draw an arrow $x\to y$ whenever $x<y$: 1→2, 1→3, 2→3.
$x=1$: there is an arrow out, so a witness $y$ exists (for example 2).
$x=2$: witness $y=3$.
$x=3$: no arrow leaves 3 (nothing is larger). No witness.
One failing $x$ is enough to make '$\forall x$' false. The negation $\exists x\,\forall y\,\neg(x<y)$ is true, with witness $x=3$.
examples.answer: False. The element 3 has no larger element in the domain.

examples.setup: How many binary relations $R$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ satisfy $\exists x\,\forall y\,R(x,y)$ (some element is related to everything)?
steps: A relation is a $3\times3$ table of 0/1, so there are $2^9=512$ relations.
Count the opposite: no row is all 1s. Each row has $2^3=8$ patterns; the all-1s pattern is the only bad one, so 7 patterns per row are allowed.
The 3 rows are independent: $7^3=343$ relations have no all-1s row.
Satisfying: $512-343=169$.
examples.answer: 169 relations.

examples.setup: Does the sentence 'every element has an $R$-successor, no element is related to itself, and $R$ is transitive' have a finite model?
steps: Without transitivity it does: on $\{1,2\}$ take $R=\{(1,2),(2,1)\}$. Every element has a successor and none is related to itself.
With transitivity, $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ force $(1,1)$, which is forbidden.
In general: start at any element and follow successors. In a finite domain you must revisit an element, and transitivity then gives $R(a,a)$, a contradiction.
So no finite model exists. The infinite order $(\mathbb N,<)$ is a model.
examples.answer: No finite model. Every model of the sentence is infinite.

cards.why: Domain questions are about checking quickly, not proving in general. In GATE: evaluate a sentence on a small domain, count the relations that satisfy it, or argue about the size of a model.
how: Fix the domain. Turn $\forall$ into AND and $\exists$ into OR.
Draw the relation as arrows or as a 0/1 table.
Check the outer quantifier first, then the inner one, element by element.
To count relations, count the tables with the row condition. Use the complement when it is simpler.
For 'smallest model' or 'finite model' questions, look for a forced infinite chain.
cards.mistake: Checking only some elements and declaring a $\forall$ statement true, or finding one failing element and declaring an $\exists$ statement false. $\forall$ needs every element; $\exists$ needs just one witness.
edge_cases: Changing the domain (adding or removing an element) can change the truth value.
A relation on an $n$-element domain has $n^2$ pairs, so $2^{n^2}$ relations.
$\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ on $\{1,2\}$ allows $(2^2-1)^2=9$ relations: every row needs at least one 1.
A sentence with only $\exists$ quantifiers can be satisfied by a model with at most that many elements.
connections: Foundations: **Sets and logic** (found.sets_logic) covers the symbols and the idea of true and false statements.
The pigeonhole idea for finite models is the same argument as for cycles in graphs.
The count of relations ties to **Sets and relations** (counting relations) and to **Counting** (complement).

scenes.title: Building a truth table column by column

steps.caption: Two variables give 4 rows. Each row is one possible world for p and q.
Column p∨q is true when at least one of p, q is true. Only the last row (both false) is false.
Column p∧q is true only when both are true: just the first row.
Column ¬(p∧q) flips the previous column.
AND the columns p∨q and ¬(p∧q). The result is true exactly when p and q differ (exclusive or).

set.text: result: true in TF and FT

scenes.title: Implication, contrapositive and converse side by side

steps.caption: Two variables, 4 rows. We compare three implications.
Column p→q is false only in row TF: the promise "if p then q" breaks when p happens and q does not.
Column ¬q→¬p (the contrapositive) is also false only in row TF. It has the same column, so it is equivalent to p→q.
Column q→p (the converse) is false in row FT instead. Different column, so it is **not** equivalent.
One more equivalent form: p→q is false only when ¬p is false and q is false, so p→q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.

scenes.title: Always true, always false, or in between

steps.caption: Four rows for (p, q). We test three formulas A, B, C and ask: always true, always false, or in between?
A is true in every row: a **tautology**. Whichever way p and q go, one of the two implications holds.
B is false in every row: a **contradiction**. It needs p or q true, yet also both false.
C is false in one row (TT) and true in three: **satisfiable but not a tautology**.

scenes.title: "Only if" points from the condition that needs a reason

objects.text: forbidden case: c true and r false
"c only if r" is not "r only if c"

steps.caption: Name the atoms: r = "it rains" and c = "the match is cancelled".
"c only if r": the match can be cancelled only when it rains. Draw the arrow from c to r, which is **c → r**.
The one broken case is c true and r false: cancelled on a dry day. That is exactly the row where c → r fails.
Compare "if it rains, the match is cancelled", which is **r → c**. The arrow points the other way, so it is a different statement.

scenes.title: A student with no line is the witness that breaks "for all"

steps.caption: Statement S: "every student passed some exam", which is $\forall s\,\exists e\,\mathrm{Passed}(s,e)$. A line means "passed".
Check every student for a line. s1 has lines to a and b. s2 has a line to a. Both pass the test.
s3 has no line at all. One student without a line breaks "for all students", so S is **false**.
Negation flips each quantifier and negates the inside: $\exists s\,\forall e\,\neg\mathrm{Passed}(s,e)$. Some student passed nothing. The witness is s3.

scenes.title: All birds fly: why the arrow, not the "and"

objects.text: B(x): x is a bird.   F(x): x can fly.

steps.caption: Domain: sparrow, eagle, bat, rock. Fill in B (is a bird) and F (can fly) for each one.
"All birds fly" is $\forall x\,(B(x)\to F(x))$. Fill the B→F row. For bat and rock, B is false, so the arrow is true automatically.
Every cell of the B→F row is T. So "all birds fly" is **true** in this domain.
The tempting $\forall x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$ says every item is a flying bird. The bat and the rock break it, so it is false here.
Rule: $\forall$ goes with $\to$, $\exists$ goes with $\wedge$. "Some bird flies" is $\exists x\,(B(x)\wedge F(x))$: true, with witness sparrow.

scenes.title: Pulling a quantifier out: the antecedent flips it

steps.caption: Domain {1, 2, 3}. $P(x)$ means "x is even": F, T, F. $W$ is one fixed fact with no x in it. Say $W$ is false.
Row $P(x)\to W$: T, F, T. It fails only at x = 2, where $P$ is true but $W$ is false.
So $\forall x\,(P(x)\to W)$ is **false**, because x = 2 fails.
Now $(\exists x\,P(x))\to W$. There is an even number (x = 2), so $\exists x\,P(x)$ is true. True → false is false. Same value.
Rule: a $\forall$ over an implication whose **antecedent** holds $x$ becomes $\exists$ once you pull it outside. W has no x, so it can move out.

scenes.title: Testing a sentence on a small domain, one x at a time

steps.caption: Domain {1, 2, 3}. Draw an arrow x → y whenever x < y: 1→2, 1→3, 2→3. Question: is $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x<y)$ true?
Test x = 1. An arrow leaves 1 (to 2 or to 3). A witness y exists, for example y = 2.
Test x = 2. An arrow leaves 2, to 3. Witness y = 3.
Test x = 3. No arrow leaves 3, because nothing in the domain is larger. There is no witness.
One failing x breaks "for all x". So the statement is **false** in this domain. Its negation $\exists x\,\forall y\,\neg(x<y)$ is true, with witness x = 3.
